knowledge_base.fact: Yeast dies at temperatures above 140°F because heat denatures essential enzymes.
The Maillard reaction begins at 285°F, creating complex flavor compounds between amino acids and sugars.
Salt denatures myosin proteins in meat, allowing them to hold more water and stay juicy.
Adding acid (like lemon juice) to beans prevents pectin breakdown, making them stay firm longer.
Baking soda (alkaline) speeds up the Maillard reaction by increasing the pH of the food surface.
Starch granules swell and burst (gelatinization) between 140°F and 158°F, thickening liquids.
Cold water is better for making pie crust because it prevents the butter from melting and hydrating the flour too early.
Honey is hygroscopic, meaning it absorbs moisture from the air, keeping baked goods moist.
Capsaicin in chili peppers is fat-soluble, which is why milk or oil eases the burn better than water.
Resting meat allows the muscle fibers to relax and reabsorb juices that were squeezed out during cooking.
Pineapple and papaya contain enzymes (bromelain/papain) that break down proteins, effectively 'digesting' meat if marinated too long.
Potatoes should be started in cold water so the outside doesn't overcook before the starch in the center gelatinizes.
Egg yolks act as emulsifiers because they contain lecithin, a molecule with one water-loving and one fat-loving end.
Sugar acts as a tenderizer in baking by interfering with gluten development and slowing protein coagulation.
Chlorophyll turns dull olive-green in acid because hydrogen ions replace the magnesium atom in the molecule.
Adding salt to water increases its boiling point (boiling point elevation), though the effect is negligible for small amounts.
High altitudes have lower atmospheric pressure, causing water to boil at lower temperatures and dough to rise faster.
The 'smell' of old fish comes from TMAO breaking down into TMA; acids like lemon juice neutralize this alkaline amine.
Sourdough bread is sour because Lactobacilli bacteria produce lactic and acetic acids during fermentation.
Garlic produces its pungent smell only when the cell walls are damaged, allowing the enzyme alliinase to react with alliin.
Deep frying relies on the Leidenfrost effect, where steam escaping the food creates a barrier that prevents oil absorption.
Onions make you cry because they release a gas (LF-synthase) that reacts with the water in your eyes to form sulfuric acid.
Whipping egg whites creates a protein network that traps air; fat (from yolk or oil) collapses this structure.
Caramelization is the pyrolysis of sugar (no proteins involved), occurring above 320°F.
Vinegar or lemon juice prevents potatoes from turning brown by lowering the pH and slowing enzyme activity.
Cold eggs separate more easily than warm eggs because the yolk membrane is firmer when cold.
Salt is a flavor 'suppressor'; it specifically suppresses bitterness, making other flavors like sweetness seem stronger.
Meringue is stabilized by Copper (like copper bowls) because it forms a bond with conalbumin, preventing over-whipping.
Al dente pasta has a core of ungelatinized starch, providing a firmer texture.
Green potatoes contain solanine, a toxic glycoalkaloid that develops alongside chlorophyll when exposed to light.
Cast iron retains heat well because it is dense and has high volumetric heat capacity, despite being a poor conductor.
Tears are avoided by chilling onions, which slows down the chemical reaction that creates the volatile gas.
The 'crust' on bread is formed by the rapid evaporation of water on the surface, concentrating sugars for Maillard.
Gelatin is derived from collagen; when heated in water, it uncoils and then forms a grid that traps liquid as it cools.
Coffee is naturally acidic (pH 5); adding a pinch of salt can neutralize the perception of bitterness.
Browning in sliced apples is caused by polyphenol oxidase reacting with oxygen (enzymatic browning).
Cream of tartar is an acid that prevents sugar crystals from forming in syrups by 'inverting' the sugar.
Freezing food doesn't kill bacteria; it merely puts them in a dormant state until thawed.
Mushrooms contain chitin in their cell walls, which is heat-stable and makes them almost impossible to overcook.
Dark pans absorb more radiant heat than light pans, leading to faster browning on the bottom of baked goods.
A raw potato can absorb excess salt from a soup via osmosis, though it is more effective at absorbing liquid than salt alone.
Kneading dough develops gluten by aligning gliadin and glutenin proteins into long, elastic chains.
Milk curdles in acid because the change in pH causes casein proteins to clump together.
Tempering chocolate involves melting it to specific temperatures to form Type V cocoa butter crystals for a glossy finish.
The 'pop' of popcorn occurs when moisture inside the kernel turns to steam, creating pressure that ruptures the hull.
Adding alcohol to sorbet lowers the freezing point, resulting in a softer, smoother texture.
Ceviche 'cooks' fish using citric acid, which denatures proteins similarly to heat but without the high temperature.
Red cabbage changes color based on pH; it turns red in acid, purple when neutral, and blue/green in alkaline environments.
Steam is a more efficient heat transfer medium than dry air because of the latent heat of vaporization.
Aging beef allows natural enzymes (calpains) to break down tough connective tissues.
Baking powder contains both an acid and a base; it reacts twice—once when wet and once when heated.
Washing rice removes excess surface starch (amylopectin), preventing the grains from sticking together.
Cooking oil smoke point is the temperature at which fats begin to break down into glycerol and free fatty acids.
The 'ring' on smoked meat is a reaction between meat pigment (myoglobin) and carbon monoxide/nitric oxide from the wood.
Butter is a 'water-in-fat' emulsion (roughly 80% fat, 15% water).
Sweating onions involves low heat to soften the cellulose without triggering the Maillard reaction.
Asparagus makes urine smell because of the breakdown of asparagusic acid into sulfur-containing compounds.
Stale bread is caused by retrogradation, where starch molecules realign into a crystalline structure, pushing water out.
Adding a pinch of sugar to tomato sauce doesn't reduce acidity (pH); it merely balances the flavor perception of sourness.
Saffron is the world's most expensive spice because it is the hand-harvested stigma of the Crocus flower.
Whipping cream works because fat globules form a protective 'cage' around air bubbles; too much whipping turns it into butter.
The green ring around hard-boiled egg yolks is iron sulfide, caused by overcooking and high heat.
Potassium bitartrate (Cream of Tartar) helps stabilize egg foams by lowering the pH and preventing protein over-bonding.
Vinegar in poaching water helps egg whites coagulate faster, keeping the egg in a neat shape.
Vanilla extract is an alcohol-based solution that dissolves the flavor compound vanillin.
Freezer burn occurs through sublimation—when ice turns directly into water vapor, dehydrating the food surface.
Tofu is made by curdling soy milk with a coagulant like calcium sulfate or magnesium chloride.
Marinating meat only penetrates a few millimeters deep; the main benefit is surface seasoning and enzyme action.
Broccoli and Brussels sprouts contain glucosinolates, which produce bitter sulfur smells if overcooked.
Convection ovens cook faster because they use fans to remove the 'boundary layer' of cool air around food.
Umami is the taste of glutamates, which are found naturally in soy sauce, parmesan, and mushrooms.
Dough 'rests' to allow gluten to relax, making it easier to roll out without it springing back.
Searing meat does not 'seal in juices'; it is done purely for the flavor of the Maillard reaction.
Adding salt to ice lowers its melting point, allowing the brine to get colder than 32°F for ice cream making.
Bitterness in cucumbers is often concentrated in the skin and ends due to cucurbitacins.
Cooking spinach significantly reduces its volume because its cell walls collapse and release water.
Fresh ginger contains proteases that can prevent gelatin from setting if added raw to jellies.
Microwaves heat food by causing water molecules to rotate rapidly (dipolar rotation), generating friction/heat.
The 'bloom' on chocolate is either sugar or fat migrating to the surface, often due to temperature fluctuations.
Sous vide cooking uses a water bath to maintain a precise temperature, preventing overcooking and ensuring edge-to-edge doneness.
Honey never spoils because of its low moisture content and acidic pH (around 3.9).
Hard water (high in calcium) can toughen vegetables by reinforcing the pectin in their cell walls.
The smell of rain (petrichor) is sometimes mimicked in beet flavor due to the compound geosmin.
Browning in butter (beurre noisette) is the Maillard reaction of the milk solids (proteins and sugars).
Washing mushrooms doesn't make them soggy; they are already 90% water and absorb very little surface moisture.
Bread dough rises because yeast consumes sugar and releases carbon dioxide gas, which is trapped by gluten.
Potatoes stored in the fridge turn sweet because cold temperatures trigger the conversion of starch into sugar.
Pressure cookers raise the boiling point of water to 250°F, significantly speeding up chemical reactions.
The heat of a habanero is measured in Scoville Heat Units (SHU), based on the concentration of capsaicinoids.
Adding oil to pasta water does not prevent sticking; only stirring and plenty of water do.
Acrylamide is a chemical that can form in starchy foods during high-temperature cooking like frying or baking.
Lactose-free milk is made by adding the enzyme lactase, which breaks lactose into glucose and galactose.
A pinch of salt in cream can help it whip faster by destabilizing the fat globule membranes.
Balsamic vinegar gets its dark color and sweetness from years of evaporation and aging in wooden barrels.
Artichokes contain cynarin, which makes the next thing you eat or drink taste sweet.
The crackling sound of roasting meat is the sound of water pockets vaporizing and rupturing tissue.
Caffeine is a natural pesticide produced by coffee plants to paralyze or kill insects.
The bubbles in champagne are formed by dissolved carbon dioxide escaping at 'nucleation sites' like dust or scratches on the glass.
Freezing blueberries can increase their antioxidant availability by breaking down plant tissue.
Clarifying butter removes water and milk solids, raising the smoke point from 350°F to 450°F.
